short: The largest public baths built in Rome to that date, opened in 216 CE, could serve 1,600 bathers at once.
full:
Caracalla began the great bath complex south of the Aventine Hill around 212 CE, brick stamps having ruled out an earlier start under his father Septimius Severus, and dedicated it in 216. The main block alone covered about 25 hectares, its central hall vaulted in concrete over 33 metres high, with a sequence of cold, warm and hot bathing rooms, an open-air pool, exercise courts and libraries wrapped in an outer precinct of gardens and lecture spaces. An underground network of tunnels moved fuel and slaves servicing dozens of furnaces without disrupting the bathers above.

Caracalla was assassinated in 217, but work continued under his successors and the complex was substantially finished under Severus Alexander by 235. It functioned until the Ostrogothic siege of 537 cut Rome's aqueducts, after which it fell into ruin. Its surviving vaulted halls later inspired the design of large nineteenth- and twentieth-century public buildings, including railway terminals, that needed to enclose comparably vast unsupported spans.
